newsitem.title: UK: Russia Eurobond maturity to be five years - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Russia Eurobond maturity to be five years - dealers.

text.p: Details on Russia's upcoming debut Eurobond were beginning to firm up, with syndicate managers expecting it to issue a five-year bond for up to $500 million.
"Now that Russia has got ratings, which were better than expected, a five-year maturity is plausible," said an emerging market syndicate manager at a European bank.
"The fear was the rating would be much lower which would have made a three-year maturity the only option," he said.
On Monday, three international rating agencies assigned Russia long-term foreign currency debt ratings, all in the speculative grade double-B category.
Moody's gave it a Ba2 rating, Standard & Poor's assigned it a BB-minus and IBCA awarded Russia a BB-plus.
The size of the deal, which traders said was expected in the first week of November or perhaps even earlier, was still subject to debate.
The indicated $300 million to $500 million range still stood, although the relatively strong ratings made the higher end feasible, dealers said.
"Russia could raise $500 million, which would be a good size for a benchmark, but anything above that would be too large," said a Russia specialist at a U.S. bank.
The next big question is the pricing.
One dealer said Russia did not want to pay a coupon above 10 percent, and this was being considered before looking at a launch spread.
"The talk is Russia does not want to pay a coupon in the double-digits," said the European bank's syndicate manager.
"The actual spread at which the deal is launched will then depend on whether Russia launches a Eurobond with an annual coupon, or a 144A structure with a semi-annual coupon," he said.
At current market yields, a five-year Eurobond would pay 350 basis points over U.S. Treasuries if the coupon did not exceed 10 percent.
A five-year 144A bond would pay a 375 b.p. spread with the same 10 percent coupon, paid semi-annually.
"Optically, the structure makes a difference, with one spread lower due to annualisation of the coupon," the syndicate manager said.
Other traders said a launch spread of around 400 b.p. over Treasuries was likely.
Although there are a number of other emerging market borrowers with ratings similar to those received by Russia, most outstanding five-year paper was illiquid, dealers said.
Argentina, which is rated B1/BB-, has a five-year global bond outstanding. It was launched at 410 b.p. over in February, and now trades at 340 b.p. over.
"Demand for Latin American paper and Eastern European paper is very different, so even if the ratings are the same it is hard to compare," said a debt trader.
"Russia will be setting a benchmark, and the pricing will have to worked out to reflect its new status and the uncertainty surrounding investment there," he said.
The lead managers of Russia's debut issue are J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg, who declined to give specific details of the transaction.
